title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarking & Runbooks
author: Asha Patel
summary: Comprehensive reference for the Redwood serving runtime team: architecture overview, kernel scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, recent release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks. This page is the canonical starting point for onboarding, incident response, and performance tuning.
content:
Overview:

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling playbook, benchmarking suite, release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended for engineers on the serving-runtime, SRE, and infra teams who operate GPU-backed inference services.

1) Architecture overview

- Purpose: provide a high-level view of the inference serving runtime and component responsibilities.
- Key components:
  - Front-end routing (router-service): consistent API, authentication, request validation, per-tenant routing policy.
  - Dispatcher: implements request sharding, per-request routing policy, and pre-routing validation (size, model compatibility, TTL).
  - Serving runtime (runtime-worker): GPU-backed process that hosts model weights, executes kernels, manages KV cache, and exposes a local RPC for token streaming.
  - Placement & autoscaler (placement-controller): maintains GPU pools, assigns model shards, and executes scaling policies for Dedicated and Private modes.
  - KV/Prefix cache (cache-service): Redis-backed prefix cache with LRU + TTL and a GPU-aware hot-set promotion path.
  - Telemetry pipeline (telemetry-proxy -> metrics-pipeline): token-level latency/cost breakdown, sample traces, and error logs.

- Data flow (short): client -> router-service -> dispatcher -> runtime-worker(s) -> (cache, telemetry).

Design goals and constraints:
- Predictable P99 latency target: 150ms for 512-token responses on p4/rt-optimized pools for hosted tier (configurable per-customer).
- Cost-aware routing: minimize per-token GPU cost while meeting latency SLO via model variants and batching policies.
- Graceful degradation: automatic fallback to smaller/quantized variants when capacity constrained.

Ownership and interfaces:
- router-service: ownership: api-platform. RPC: GRPC v2 with route metadata header X-Route-Policy.
- runtime-worker: ownership: serving-runtime. Local RPC: unix socket protobuf API (see spec: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-reference-2027-03-04.json).

2) Kernel scheduling and execution model

Goals:
- Maximize GPU utilization without violating latency SLOs.
- Minimize kernel launch overhead and maximize batch coalescing.

Scheduling layers:
- Request prioritization: requests annotated with priority levels (real-time, standard, background). Real-time has preemptive reservation.
- Micro-batching: per-worker continuous batching pipeline. Batching window default: 4ms (configurable per pool).
- Kernel fusion / stream management: use N streams per GPU (default 4) where affinity maps model attention kernels to streams to allow overlapped IO + compute.
- KV cache placement: warm KV lives in GPU pinned memory; cold prefix served from CPU memory with async prefetching.

Important heuristics and configs (examples):
- Batch sizing policy: target_batch_size = clamp(estimate_optimal(T), 1, 32) where estimate is based on recent median sequence length and model flops.
- Latency headroom guard: if P99(latency) > 0.85 * SLO, temporarily reduce batch window by 50% and raise real-time priority share.

Kernel selection and fallback:
- Kernel table: runtime queries a compiled kernel table keyed by (model-arch, dtype, seq_len_bucket, device_capability). The table selects the optimal kernel binary variant.
- Fallback: if optimized kernel OOMs at runtime, fallback to safe kernel with lower memory pressure and emit alert with trace_id.

3) Profiling playbook (how-to run and interpret profiles)

When to profile:
- New model onboarding.
- Unexpected latency regressions or increased GPU memory OOMs.
- Before/after compiler/kernel updates.

Quick profiling steps:
1) Reproduce workload: use curated trace from benchmarking-suite (see section 4) that matches the customer workload profile.
2) Run profiler (containerized):
   - Snapshot command (example):
     sudo ./tools/profile/runtime_profile.sh --model my-model:v3 --trace traces/voice_assistant.json --duration 300 --out /tmp/profile_my-model.json
   - The profiler records kernel timelines, memcpy, queueing delays, and host-side serialization times.
3) Upload profile to analysis service:
   - curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -F 'file=@/tmp/profile_my-model.json' https://telemetry.internal/profiles/upload
4) Inspect profile with flame view: open /internal-tools/profile-viewer and filter by trace_id.

Profiling checklist (interpreting results):
- Host serialization: high CPU times in serialize_request -> consider moving preprocessing to edge or increase serialization worker pool.
- memcpy peaks: frequent memcpy peaks between host and device indicate small-batch churn—increase batching window or use pinned memory pooling.
- Kernel tail latency: long tail on attention kernels suggests memory thrashing or poor kernel fit; check kernel table mapping and try alternative kernel variants.
- KV cache misses: high miss rate indicates hot-set misconfiguration; increase hot-set promotion threshold or adjust cache TTLs.

Recommended tooling and flags:
- nvprof/nvtx spans integrated via profiler script.
- runtime worker flags for debug profiling: --profile-kernels --profile-interval-ms=1000 --emit-nvtx

4) Benchmarking suite (what to run, metrics, and automation)

Purpose:
- Validate performance guarantees, regression detection, and generate tuning recommendations.

Contents:
- Workload traces: standard (conversational), long-seq (document-qa), embeddings, short-stateless (search). Traces recorded from production with PII scrubbed.
- Harnesses: load-generator (go-based), latency-harness (python), memory/stability testers.
- Baseline profiles: golden-results directory containing baseline P50/P95/P99 latency and tokens/s for each model/pool.

Key metrics collected:
- Latency percentiles per token and per-request (P50/P95/P99).
- GPU utilization and SM efficiency.
- Memory high-water marks and OOM counts.
- Token throughput (tokens/sec) and cost-per-token estimate.
- Batching characteristics: average batch size, batch window distribution.

Automated CI integration:
- Benchmarks run nightly against a stable commit on a dedicated perf cluster.
- Regression alerting: if P95 increases > 10% from baseline or OOMs introduced, open perf/regression ticket with tag perf/regress.

How to run a local benchmark (example):
- Start a local runtime on dev GPU: docker-compose -f docker/dev-runtime.yml up --build -d
- Run harness: ./benchmarks/run_benchmark.py --trace traces/standard_conversation.json --duration 600 --pool local-dev --out results/local_standard.json
- Summarize: python benchmarks/summarize.py results/local_standard.json

5) Release notes (recent notable changes)

2027-08-20 (v2027.8.20):
- Introduced per-pool continuous batching heuristics (adaptive window) which reduced median tokens/sec cost by ~8% on p4 pools.
- Kernel table expansion: added fused-attention-optimized kernel for gpt-ish models (seq_len <= 1024).
- Telemetry: added token-level cost attribution to metrics pipeline.

2027-08-30 (v2027.8.30):
- Fixed regression causing KV cache promotions to stall under multi-tenant contention.
- Default micro-batch window reduced from 6ms to 4ms for hosted pools to improve P99 latency.

Guidance for rolling releases:
1) Canary rollout: enable feature flag in placement-controller for 5% of traffic tiered by customer size.
2) Monitor: P50/P95/P99 latency, GPU OOMs, and batch-size distributions for 2 hours.
3) Rollback: revert flag in placement-controller and redeploy runtime-worker with previous kernel table if regressions exceed thresholds (defined below).

Rollout thresholds (abort criteria):
- P99 latency increased by > 15% over baseline for > 5 minutes.
- Any new OOM introduced in > 0.1% of requests over 10 minutes.
- Batch size distribution shifts causing > 25% increase in small-batch (< 4) fraction.

6) Known issues (current)

- Issue #1073: Intermittent OOMs when serving large-seq (>=2048 tokens) with fused kernels on devices with 40GB. Workaround: pin model to safe-kernel in placement-controller. Status: investigation in progress; mitigation released 2027-08-30.
- Issue #1138: Telemetry pipeline drop under extreme ingress (DDoS-like) causes incomplete token-level traces. Workaround: increase telemetry-proxy buffer and enable sample-based tracing. Status: patched in v2027.8.30; long-term fix planned Q4.
- Issue #1212: On some NVLink topologies kernel-launch serialization causes excess host CPU usage. Workaround: reduce runtime worker concurrency or set --kernel-launch-async=true. Status: tracking; perf tuning recommended per-cluster.

7) Operational runbooks

Runbook: High P99 latency (Realtime traffic)
- Owner: serving-runtime SRE oncall.
- Symptoms: P99 latency > SLO for > 2 minutes on real-time priority traffic.
- Steps:
  1) Check live dashboard (dashboards/serving/runtime/p99-latency): confirm spike and scope (model, pool, region).
  2) Inspect last 30m traces for affected trace_id(s) in profile-viewer.
  3) Check batch-size distribution: kubectl exec -it runtime-worker-<pod> -- /bin/runtime-admin stats | grep batch
  4) If batch window increased unexpectedly: reduce by updating pool config: curl -X PATCH -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" https://placement.internal/pools/<pool>/config -d '{"batch_window_ms":4}'
  5) If GPU OOMs present: set placement override to safe-kernel for affected model: curl -X POST https://placement.internal/override -d '{"model":"my-model","kernel":"safe-kernel"}'
  6) Open incident ticket and notify oncall-channel #serving-runtime.

Runbook: GPU OOM storm
- Owner: serving-runtime oncall + infra.
- Symptoms: sudden spike in OOMs across a pool.
- Steps:
  1) Quarantine pool: put pool in drain mode in placement-controller UI to prevent new assignments.
  2) Scale up with emergency capacity or move critical traffic to dedicated fallback pools.
  3) Collect kernel traces for failing requests and upload for analysis.
  4) Rollback recent kernel-table or runtime-worker image if OOMs correlate with a recent deploy.

Appendix: Useful commands & snippets

- Dump runtime metrics quickly:
  kubectl logs -l app=runtime-worker --tail 200 | jq -r '.metrics' | tail -n 100

- Toggle canary flag for placement-controller:
  ./scripts/flip_canary.sh --flag adaptive-batching --pct 5 --env prod

- Example kernel-table entry (YAML):
  - model: gpt-medium
    dtype: fp16
    seq_len_bucket: 1-512
    kernel: fused-attn-v2
    notes: "Use for interactive traffic; falls back to safe-attn if OOM"

Maintainers and escalation
- Primary owners: serving-runtime team (rotation roster in team wiki).
- Escalation: serving-runtime oncall -> infra oncall -> SRE manager.

Document maintenance
- This page is the canonical combined reference. Major updates (architecture changes, SLO updates, or new kernels) should include an entry in the release notes block above and notify reviewers.
